title: Knowledge Check 7 - Lessons 31-35
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 31-35 - Harmonization and Unification | Data Enhancements, Sharing, and Analysis. Pass with 80% or higher to move toward unlocking the cert prep exam.

questions.question: How does a Data Lake Object relate to a Data Model Object?
options: The Data Lake Object is the harmonized model object.
The Data Lake Object is the raw, stream-shaped table that must be mapped onto a Data Model Object to become model data.
They are two names for the same object.
A Data Lake Object cannot be mapped to a model object.
questions.explanation: A DLO is the staging layer that mirrors the source; mapping its fields to a DMO turns them into model attributes. They are distinct layers, and mapping a DLO to a DMO is exactly how data reaches the model.

questions.question: A stream loaded successfully, but its records never appear in identity resolution. What is the most likely cause?
options: The Data Lake Object has too many fields.
The Individual ID was never mapped from a populated source column.
The org reached a Data Model Object limit.
Identity resolution is turned off.
questions.explanation: Even with data loaded, an unmapped or empty Individual ID means the record cannot join to a person, so identity resolution skips it. Field count, a DMO limit, and a disabled ruleset do not match the described symptom.

questions.question: An architect must use data already ingested in a Data Lake Object for a second Data Model Object without reloading it. What do they do?
options: Re-ingest an identical stream.
Add a second mapping from the existing Data Lake Object to the target Data Model Object.
Clone the Data Lake Object.
Query the DLO and reload it through an API.
questions.explanation: You can map an existing DLO to an additional DMO without re-ingesting, which reuses the staged data. Re-ingesting, cloning, and API reloads either duplicate data or waste effort for a result the mapping step already provides.

questions.question: When is a custom Data Model Object the right choice over adding fields to a standard object?
options: Never, standard objects are fixed.
When the data is organization-specific and does not fit a standard subject area, and you also define its relationships into the model.
Whenever you need to store any new field.
Only in a sandbox.
questions.explanation: Custom objects are for genuinely distinct data that a standard subject area does not cover, and they must be wired into the model with relationships. Standard objects can be extended with fields, so 'never' and 'any new field' are both wrong, and there is no sandbox-only rule.

questions.question: A custom Data Model Object holds the right rows but never appears in segments about people. What is the most likely gap?
options: It needs a page layout.
Its relationship to Individual, and the mapped Individual ID key, is missing, so records are not tied to a person.
Custom objects cannot be used in segments.
It must be converted into a standard object.
questions.explanation: Without the relationship to Individual and a populated Individual ID, the custom object's records never attach to a person, so person-based segments exclude them. Page layouts do not apply here, custom objects can be segmented once joined, and conversion is not required.

questions.question: For a custom Data Model Object to contribute to identity resolution, what must be true?
options: It must be a standard object first.
It must be referenced by the identity resolution ruleset, with its relevant key fields populated.
It must be a Data Lake Object.
Identity resolution includes every object automatically.
questions.explanation: Identity resolution considers only the objects the ruleset names, and matching needs populated keys, so a referenced object with populated keys can contribute. Nothing is included automatically, and neither the object type nor a conversion makes it match.

questions.question: After unification, a segment shows duplicate profiles for what should be the same customer. Which modeling decision most likely explains it?
options: Too many engagement objects.
Inconsistent Individual ID formatting or keys across sources, so the same person never matched.
Too few fields on the Individual object.
The segment is scheduled at the wrong time.
questions.explanation: Matching depends on a consistently populated, consistently formatted Individual ID; small differences across sources split one person into several profiles. Object counts, field counts, and schedule do not cause duplicate profiles.

questions.question: Which pair of modeling choices most directly protects most-recent-value logic and correct monetary aggregates?
options: Page layouts and profiles.
Timestamps mapped for freshness, and a currency field stored with amounts.
More custom fields on each object.
Larger data streams with more columns.
questions.explanation: Timestamps let Data 360 choose the freshest value and order events, and a currency alongside the amount keeps aggregates comparable. Layouts and profiles are unrelated, and more fields or columns do not fix currency or freshness problems.

questions.question: Where should format standardization, such as dates, phone numbers, and text casing, ideally happen for a Data 360 model?
options: Inside every downstream segment.
At or before mapping, during stream field mapping and transformation.
Never, because Data 360 standardizes everything automatically.
Only in each source system's user interface.
questions.explanation: Normalizing at mapping time makes the fix reproducible across every consumer. Doing it per segment is not reproducible, automatic standardization of arbitrary source formats is not something to rely on, and relying on source UIs leaves the model inconsistent.

questions.question: Which insight type processes high-volume batches of stored records to produce multidimensional metrics that segment criteria and personalization attributes can read?
options: Streaming Insight
Calculated Insight
Real-Time Insight
An identity resolution ruleset
questions.explanation: Calculated Insights run high-volume batches over stored data and publish measures and dimensions consumed by segments and personalization, while streaming and real-time insights work on engagement events.

questions.question: A team needs a rolling one-minute time series aggregation of Web SDK engagement events to trigger a data action. Which insight type fits?
options: Calculated Insight
Copy field enrichment
Streaming Insight
Data transform
questions.explanation: Streaming Insights aggregate near real-time engagement events over a rolling window and drive orchestration or data actions, while calculated insights are batch and a data transform shapes data rather than aggregating events.

questions.question: Which statement distinguishes Real-Time Insights from Streaming Insights?
options: Real-Time Insights compute results in milliseconds from each event that updates a real-time data graph
Real-Time Insights run only on mapped data lake object aggregations
Real-Time Insights replace identity resolution
Real-Time Insights are a type of copy field enrichment
questions.explanation: Real-time insights compute per event inside a real-time data graph with millisecond results, while streaming insights summarize a rolling window, and neither replaces identity resolution nor acts as an enrichment.

questions.question: A calculated insight must produce one lifetime value per customer for a personalization attribute. What must the insight group by?
options: The order date dimension
The Individual dimension so each row is a person
No dimension, for a single overall total
The product category dimension
questions.explanation: Grouping by the Individual dimension yields one row per person, which is the form a profile-level metric and personalization attribute require, while category or date groupings describe groups rather than people.

questions.question: Which pair correctly defines a measure and a dimension in a calculated insight?
options: Measure is the field you group by; dimension is the metric function
Measure is the metric function applied to a field; dimension is the attribute you group the measure by
Both are metric functions applied to the base object
Measure is a page layout; dimension is a record type
questions.explanation: A calculated insight computes a measure, a metric function applied to a field, grouped by dimensions, the grouping attributes, so the options that swap these roles or use non-insight concepts are wrong.

questions.question: Which statement about where a calculated insight result can be used is TRUE?
options: It exists only for display and cannot be consumed elsewhere
It publishes a reusable insight object that segment criteria, personalization attributes, copy field enrichments, and data graphs can read
It can be used once and is then discarded
It serves as a replacement for identity resolution
questions.explanation: The insight object is reusable across segment criteria, attributes, enrichments, and data graphs, so re-running the definition updates consumers, and it is not display-only, single-use, or a substitute for identity resolution.
